\chapter{The Field and the Well}
\label{ch:hi-the-field-and-the-well}
\hlchaptermodality{66}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five things in a Hindi field before I take my leave.}

Complete HI-C66-well and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bīj]{\hi{बीज} (bīj) — a seed}

\label{lesson:HI-C66-seed}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{adab} mean, and what did \emph{bharosā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{बीज}}
\textbf{\hi{बीज}} (\emph{bīj}) — \textquotedblleft{}a seed\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \hi{बीज} (\emph{bīja}), 'seed', carried into Hindi with nothing changed but the final vowel, which the schwa rule you have just learnt takes off the end.

It reaches well past the field. \hi{बीज} is the seed of a plant, the germ of an idea, and the origin of anything at all — one of a small set of Hindi words that a farmer and a philosopher both use without either sounding odd.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things a field holds.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bīj}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bīj}, then \emph{khet}, and say which one goes into the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{बीज} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a seed\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[fasal]{\hi{फ़सल} (fasal) — a crop}

\label{lesson:HI-C66-crop}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bīj} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{फ़सल}}
\textbf{\hi{फ़सल}} (\emph{fasal}) — \textquotedblleft{}a crop\textquotedblright{}.

Arabic \emph{faṣl}, whose plain sense is a division or a section — a cut piece of something larger. From there it came to name a season, and from there the thing a season yields.

North India counts its year in two of them, the winter sowing and the monsoon sowing, so \hi{फ़सल} names the harvest and the stretch of months that produced it at once. Ask a \hi{किसान} how the \hi{फ़सल} is and you have asked about the weather, the work and the money together.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{fasal}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{fasal}, then \emph{kisān}, and say who watches the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{फ़सल} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a crop\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[anāj]{\hi{अनाज} (anāj) — grain}

\label{lesson:HI-C66-grain}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{fasal} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{अनाज}}
\textbf{\hi{अनाज}} (\emph{anāj}) — \textquotedblleft{}grain\textquotedblright{}.

Usually traced to Sanskrit \hi{अन्न} (\emph{anna}), 'food', through a longer form meaning 'the food that is to be eaten'. The word for food narrowed onto the one food everything else is built around.

\hi{अनाज} is grain in the bulk sense — what is stored, weighed and sold. \hi{चावल} is one kind of it, wheat is another, and \hi{अनाज} is the sack all of them come out of.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{anāj}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{anāj}, then \emph{chāval}, and say which one is the sack
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{अनाज} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}grain\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ghās]{\hi{घास} (ghās) — grass}

\label{lesson:HI-C66-grass}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{anāj} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{घास}}
\textbf{\hi{घास}} (\emph{ghās}) — \textquotedblleft{}grass\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \hi{घास} (\emph{ghāsa}), 'fodder', on the root \hi{घस्} (\emph{ghas-}), 'to eat'. Grass is named from the eating end: it is not a plant, it is what an animal is given.

That is still how the word behaves. Cut \hi{घास} travels home on a head or a bicycle for the \hi{भैंस} and the \hi{गाय}, and the lawn sense — grass you keep and do not feed to anything — is the newer, city meaning laid on top.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ghās}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ghās}, then \emph{bhaĩs}, and say which one is waiting for the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{घास} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}grass\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kuā̃]{\hi{कुआँ} (kuā̃) — a well}

\label{lesson:HI-C66-well}



\begin{quote}
Name the 4 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{कुआँ}}
\textbf{\hi{कुआँ}} (\emph{kuā̃}) — \textquotedblleft{}a well\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{कूप} (\emph{kūpa}), 'a pit, a well'. The \emph{p} softened away and the vowel came through the nose, leaving a word you write with the moon-and-dot you learnt in the letters chapter.

\hi{कूप} has cousins a long way west: Latin \emph{cūpa}, a tub or a cask, is the same ancient word, and English \emph{cup} and \emph{coop} come down from it. A hole in the ground and a thing you drink out of, both named for being hollow.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \hi{बीज}, \hi{फ़सल}, \hi{अनाज}, \hi{घास}, \hi{कुआँ}. Enough to name a field and the water that keeps it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kuā̃}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then \emph{phir milenge}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{कुआँ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a well\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
